Paleomagnetic and Ar/ Ar age constraints on the timing of deposition of
deep-water carbonates of the Kurnool Group (Cuddapah basin) and
correlation across Proterozoic Purana successions of Southern India
Herv ´ e Waboa,*, Nicolas J. Beukesa, Sarbani Patranabis-Debb, Dilip Sahab, Georgy Belyanina,
Jan Kramersa
aDepartment of Science and Innovation – National Research Foundation Centre of Excellence for Integrated Mineral and Energy Resource Analysis (DSI-NRF CIMERA)
and Paleoproterozoic Mineralization Research Group (PPM Research Group), Department of Geology, University of Johannesburg, PO Box 524, Auckland Park 2006,
Johannesburg, South Africa
bIndian Statistical Institute, 203 Barrackpore Trunk Road, Kolkata 700 108, India
A R T I C L E I N F O A B S T R A C T
Keywords: The sedimentary basins of the Bastar and Dharwar cratons, namely Chhattisgarh, Cuddapah, Intravati, Kaladgi-
Southern Purana basins Bhima, and Pranhita-Godavari are located to the south of the Central Indian Tectonic Zone. These Southern
Deep-water carbonate Purana basins host well-preserved successions that may be divided into four unconformity-bounded sequences (i.
Narji Limestone
e., Sequences I to IV). Sequence III contains unique deep-water carbonate layers, among which the Narji
Paleomagnetism
40Ar/39Ar geochronology Limestone in the Cuddapah basin is representative. These carbonate layers have been shown to be of Meso-
proterozoic age in most basins. However, the age of the Narji Limestone is still debated. Here, we report a
primary paleomagnetic pole (26.2◦N, 063.2◦E, A95 =13.7◦) with a positive fold test from the Narji Limestone,
and also a reset 40Ar/39Ar age of ~800 Ma obtained on a glauconite. Our results, combined with existing
paleomagnetic data indicate that the Narji Limestone and Sequence III carbonates of the other Southern Purana
basins share a similar primary paleomagnetic signature. The paleomagnetic poles of these carbonates plot
consistently, and are used to calculate a mean pole (36.3◦N, 070.8◦E, A95 =10.7◦) that compares well with a
~1.19 Ga Indian pole. Our results contradict the view that Sequence III carbonates of the individual Southern
Purana basins were deposited at different times as previously inferred from geochronological data. Instead, we
suggest that these carbonates represent interconnected successions deposited in middle to late Mesoproterozoic
times during an extensive marine flooding event on the Southern India craton. Our results support the suggestion
that the existing Neoproterozoic ages for Sequence III may reflect post-depositional events.

12

### page_13
H. Wabo et al. J o u r n a l o f A s i a n E a r t h S c i e n c e s 223(2022)104984
suspiciously close to the group of poles related to the Ediacaran-
Cambrian (600 Ma-525 Ma) or the ~800 Ma magnetic overprint in
India (Fig. 9a). The latter overprint, which is also observed in the present
study (LT component; Fig. 8b), is apparently widespread from India and
was previously reported by many authors. For instance, demagnetiza-
tion of carbonates in the adjacent Kaladgi and Bhima basins (Wabo et al.,
2020) revealed secondary magnetizations likely related to this over-
print. Several authors (e.g., Belica et al., 2014; Halls et al., 2007; Piv-
arunas et al., 2019; Pradhan et al., 2008) also observed an Ediacaran-
Cambrian or ~800 Ma overprint during demagnetization of mafic
dykes, some of which are separated by more than 300 km. Based on the
above evidence, we argue that the poles of Goutham et al. (2006) are
related to younger magnetic overprints and consider our NJL paleo-
magnetic pole at this stage as the only reliable primary paleomagnetic
result for Sequence III (i.e., the Kurnool Group) of the Cuddapah basin.
The NJL paleomagnetic pole can be integrated with existing primary
paleomagnetic data from the Southern Purana basins in order to inves-
tigate the chronology of Sequence III carbonates in a manner indepen-
dent of existing age constraints. These carbonates in the Pranhita-
Godavari Valley (i.e., Chanda Limestone and Sat Nala Shale of Pen-
genga Group) and Chhattisgarh (i.e., Sarangarth Limestone of Raipur
Group) basins, which are respectively located at about 400 km and more
than 600 km in the north of our sampling area, yielded primary dual-
polarity steep components (Fig. 9b) supported by a positive reversal,
conglomerate and regional fold tests (De Kock et al., 2015). Such pri-
mary, dual-polarity, steep magnetic components were also reported by
Wabo et al. (2020) some 200–300 km west of our study area in limestone
(i.e., Konkankoppa and Katamadevarahalli limestones) and shale (i.e.,
Halkurki and Harwal shale) of Sequence III in the Kaladgi and Bhima
basins (Fig. 9b).
